newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan moves step towards central bank independence.
newsitem.headline: Japan moves step towards central bank independence.

text.p: Japan took a step towards increasing the independence of the Bank of Japan (BOJ) on Wednesday when a government committee unveiled some of its proposals for changes to a decades-old central bank law.

"I think the reform plan as a whole clearly indicates that it follows the spirit of giving more independence to the BOJ," Ryuichiro Tachi, chairman of the government subcommittee discussing BOJ law reforms, told a news conference.
The plan, which aims to free the central bank from the grip of the once-powerful Finance Ministry, is part of deregulation promoted by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

Hashimoto, himself a former finance minister, hopes to reduce the authority of MOF, which has come under fire for its handling of Japan's banking crisis and various embarrassing scandals involving its senior officials.
But sources close to the BOJ expressed doubt as to whether the measures were enough to secure full independence rivalling that of other central banks in major industrialised nations.

The members of the Financial System Research Council subcommittee agreed on Wednesday to diminish official influence over BOJ monetary policy decisions and to give legal backing to its inspection of financial institutions, Tachi said.
They also agreed to take away the right of the finance minister and Finance Ministry officials to directly inspect and order some BOJ operations.

But the government can still directly intervene in BOJ policy decisions by asking the BOJ policy-making board to delay monetary policy decisions, though the board will have the ultimate say in whether to carry them out, Tachi said.
Currently, the government can order the BOJ to postpone monetary policy decisions should the central bank's views differ from those of the government.
The members agreed that the finance minister would still be able to carry out necessary checks and receive reports through BOJ auditors should the central bank break laws or regulations, Tachi said.

Other issues agreed by the subcommittee was that the BOJ, in exchange for its independence, should disclose the summary and minutes of the policy-making board meetings after a set time period, which will be decided by board members, he said.

They also agreed that the BOJ should report to the parliament twice a year from the current once a year, and to speak on more subjects than just their financial standing, a MOF official told reporters.

The government's authority over approving BOJ budgets, seen as another key factor in gauging how much independence will be given to the central bank, which will be discussed in the next meeting which is scheduled for Friday.
They will also discuss the thorny issue of whether BOJ governor and deputy governor will need parliamentary approval for their appointments, from current cabinet approval.
MOF officials have said that the council will likely come up with its final report by early February, which will become basis for bills to be submitted to the current session of the parliament.
